EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Rapid, unplanned urbanization and recurrent high-intensity monsoon precipita-
tion severely overwhelm aging stormwater drainage infrastructures across tier-
two Indian municipalities, culminating in systemic waterlogging, structural asset
degradation, and public paralysis. Conventional municipal public works oper-
ate reactively, deploying desilting crews primarily in response to localized citizen
grievances or visible surface overflow while neglecting topological connectivity and
backwater surcharge dynamics.
This dissertation presents CivicTwin, an AI-enabled cyber-physical digital twin
developed for predictive urban drainage management and proactive flood resilience
in Vellore Municipal Corporation (CMC). CivicTwin formulates 13,998 drain con-
duits across 60 spatial zones into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) comprising
22,737 hydraulic edges. Integrating the rational runoff method, an ensemble
Random Forest blockage surrogate, and a bitset-accelerated reachability engine,
CivicTwin introduces a multi-criteria cascade-aware dispatch strategy. Across
simulated rainfall intensities from 80 to 160 mm/hr, the proposed cascade-aware
method resolves between 3.1× and 4.4× more at-risk and backwater-threatened
conduits than traditional severity-only desilting under identical municipal clearing
budgets. Implemented as an interactive web GIS command dashboard connecting
FastAPI, React-Leaflet, and PostgreSQL/PostGIS, CivicTwin provides municipal
administrators with real-time hydraulic bottleneck foresight, maximizing labor
productivity and transforming municipal disaster response into predictive urban
resilience.

Chapter 1
INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background and Context
Urban stormwater drainage systems represent critical subterranean lifeline in-
frastructures engineered to evacuate excess surface precipitation, safeguard mu-
nicipal assets, and prevent localized hydraulic inundation[cite: 80]. In rapidly
developing urban agglomerations across the Global South, particularly tier-two
Indian municipalities such as Vellore, Tamil Nadu, infrastructural expansion has
struggled to keep pace with rapid surface imperviousness and urbanization[cite:
80]. The expansion of asphalt roadways, dense concrete residential layouts, and
commercial corridors has drastically compromised natural hydrological infiltra-
tion basins, multiplying urban runoff coeﬀicients from pre-development estimates
of 0.20–0.30 to values exceeding 0.75–0.85[cite: 80].
Simultaneously, changing climatic patterns have intensified convective precip-
itation events[cite: 80]. Modern monsoon seasons are increasingly punctuated by
short-duration, high-intensity cloudburst phenomena wherein precipitation rates
regularly exceed 80 to 120 mm/hr[cite: 80]. When these acute volumetric down-
pours strike municipal drainage networks choked with unsegregated municipal
solid waste, construction debris, and heavy silt deposition, the effective hydraulic
conveyance cross-section of drainage conduits contracts drastically[cite: 80]. Wa-
ter levels rapidly breach curb-inlet thresholds, resulting in widespread flash wa-
terlogging, road surface destruction, economic paralysis, and acute vector-borne
public health hazards[cite: 80].
The Vellore City Municipal Corporation (CMC), comprising 60 administrative
wards covering diverse topography ranging from the slopes of the Eastern Ghats
down toward the Palar river basin, faces chronic inundation during the North-
east and Southwest monsoon seasons[cite: 80]. The municipal drainage network
consists of heterogeneous open roadside channels, covered masonry channels, and
buried pipe culverts built incrementally over several decades[cite: 80]. Managing
such a sprawling, subterranean network under severe municipal budget and labor
constraints remains one of the most pressing civic governance challenges in urban
engineering[cite: 80].

1.1.1 Hydro-Meteorological Context and Topographic setting of Vellore
Vellore is situated at an mean elevation of approximately 216 meters above
Mean Sea Level (MSL), bounded by rugged granitic terrain characteristics of the
Eastern Ghats[cite: 80]. The geographical positioning exposes the urban agglom-
eration to bimodal precipitation patterns:
1. Southwest Monsoon (June to September): Characterized by localized con-
vective thunder-showers and high-intensity short-duration cloudbursts[cite:
80].
2. Northeast Monsoon (October to December): Generates sustained regional
depressions that drop substantial cumulative volumetric rainfall across the
Palar river catchment basin[cite: 80].
Due to steep elevation gradients descending from hill-slope peripheral wards
(e.g., Ward 1 to Ward 12) down into central valley markets (e.g., CMC Hos-
pital zone, Long Bazaar, and Katpadi road junction), surface runoff accelerates
rapidly along upper tributaries[cite: 80]. However, as flow reaches flatter central
commercial corridors where bed slopes flatten below 0.10%, hydraulic conveyance
velocities collapse[cite: 80, 85]. This sudden hydraulic drop promotes rapid grav-
itational settling of suspended urban silt, creating chronic structural bottlenecks
that trigger extensive upstream backwater surcharges[cite: 80, 88].
1.1.2 Hydrological Challenges in Tier-Two Indian Agglomerations
Tier-two Indian cities experience unique hydro-dynamic pressures due to high
urban density coupled with legacy stormwater networks[cite: 80]. Unlike planned
metropolitan centers with dedicated subterranean storm trunks, municipal corpo-
rations in tier-two regions rely predominantly on roadside open drains designed
for low-intensity continuous rainfall[cite: 80]. Over past decades, commercial
encroachment and informal building expansion have converted permeable soil sur-
faces into continuous impervious slabs[cite: 80].
During monsoon depressions, peak discharge ( Q) arriving at roadside chan-
nels spikes within minutes of precipitation onset[cite: 80, 85]. Because time-of-
concentration ( tc) across small urban sub-catchments is short (often under 10 to
15 minutes), drainage channels receive immediate, unattenuated peak flows[cite:
80, 85]. When these channels are partially clogged by urban silt or solid waste,
local hydraulic conveyance capacity falls below peak incoming runoff, initiating
immediate surface surcharging[cite: 80, 85].

1.1.3 Infrastructural Heterogeneity of the Vellore Drainage Network
The stormwater network of Vellore Municipal Corporation reflects decades of
unsystematic infrastructural additions[cite: 80]. The network encompasses four
primary structural classifications[cite: 80]:
1. Open Concrete Channels: Standard roadside U-shaped drains engineered
for surface runoff collection along arterial and secondary roads[cite: 80].
2. Covered Masonry Drains: Brick or concrete block channels covered with
removable slab covers, prevalent in dense commercial markets such as CMC
Hospital Zone and Long Bazaar[cite: 80].
3. Buried Concrete Pipe Culverts: Circular cross-section pipes conveying flow
beneath road intersections and major transit corridors[cite: 80].
4. Natural Earthen Channels: Unlined ditches serving peripheral wards and
primary outfalls discharging toward the Palar river basin[cite: 80].
Each structural classification exhibits distinct Manning roughness coeﬀicients ( n∈
[0.013, 0.035]), cross-sectional geometries, and sediment deposition dynamics[cite:
80, 85]. Modeling such a heterogeneous network requires unifying diverse geomet-
ric parameters into a standardized hydraulic framework[cite: 80].
1.2 Problem Statement
Current municipal flood management practices in municipal corporations op-
erate predominantly in a reactive and localized operational paradigm[cite: 80]:
• Reactive Desilting Deployment: Desilting machinery, suction tankers, and
manual public works crews are conventionally mobilized only after citizen
complaints are filed via grievance portals or following visible surface inun-
dation on arterial transit corridors[cite: 80, 81].
• Topological Blindness in Prioritization: When municipal supervisors do at-
tempt proactive desilting, prioritization is guided almost exclusively by iso-
lated channel blockage ratios (e.g., clearing whatever conduit appears visu-
ally most silted)[cite: 81]. This heuristic fundamentally ignores the directed
network topology of the drainage graph[cite: 81]. A severely silted conduit
situated near a high-elevation headwater with no upstream tributaries causes
strictly localized overflow; conversely, a moderately silted conduit serving as
a primary downstream bottleneck can trigger severe backwater surcharge
and hydraulic failure across dozens or hundreds of interconnected upstream
channels[cite: 81].
3
17:
• Absence of Predictive Hydro-Informatics Tools: Municipal public works de-
partments lack accessible, real-time computational decision-support systems
that couple hydrological rainfall-runoff calculations with spatial network
topology to evaluate dynamic failure cascades before a storm arrives[cite:
81]. Full-scale hydrodynamic software packages (such as US-EPA SWMM)
demand extensive boundary parameter calibration and take hours or days
to execute over thousands of conduits, rendering them impractical for live
emergency dispatch decisions[cite: 81, 85].
Without an integrated cyber-physical digital twin capable of mapping sub-
terranean flow connectivity, predicting blockage-induced surcharge, and ranking
interventions by systemic network impact, municipal interventions remain ineﬀi-
cient, treating localized symptoms rather than hydraulic root causes[cite: 81].
1.3 Research Questions
To address these administrative and technical challenges, this dissertation in-
vestigates four fundamental research questions:
• RQ1: How can heterogeneous municipal vector data and terrain Digital
Elevation Models (DEMs) be synthesized into an elevation-enforced Directed
Acyclic Graph (DAG) that accurately enforces physical gravity flow while
eliminating topological cycles[cite: 81, 95, 96]?
• RQ2: Can bitset-accelerated transitive closure over topological sort orders
compress all-pairs reachability computations to sub-30 millisecond latencies
for real-time web decision support[cite: 82, 97, 98]?
• RQ3: How accurately can an ensemble machine learning surrogate predict
structural blockage vulnerability and hydraulic surcharge risk across contin-
uous continuous morphological feature spaces[cite: 82, 101, 102]?
• RQ4: To what degree does a multi-criteria cascade-aware dispatch optimiza-
tion strategy outperform standard municipal severity-only heuristics under
strictly constrained municipal maintenance budgets[cite: 82, 104, 105]?
1.4 Project Objectives
The primary objective of this dissertation is to design, implement, and vali-
date CivicTwin, an AI-enabled, cyber-physical digital twin that unifies geospatial
topology, hydrodynamic modeling, and machine learning surrogates into a real-
time predictive decision-support system for municipal drainage management[cite:
81]. The specific technical objectives are:

1.5 Motivation and Societal Impact
Urban drainage resilience directly intersects citizen safety, public health, and
municipal economics[cite: 82]. Flooded arterial roads paralyze public transporta-
tion, strand emergency services, and inflict substantial structural damage upon
road pavements and foundation soils, necessitating recurring multi-crore road
resurfacing expenditures[cite: 82]. Furthermore, stagnant stormwater mixed with
overflowing drainage promotes the breeding of disease vectors (such as Aedes ae-
gypti and Anopheles mosquitoes), escalating dengue, chikungunya, and malaria
outbreaks in high-density urban wards[cite: 82].

1.5.1 Socio-Economic and Infrastructure Degradation Hazards
The impact of localized urban inundation in tier-two municipalities manifests
across three distinct socio-economic dimensions[cite: 80, 82]:
• Economic Distruption: Surcharged roadside drains inundate local ground-
floor commercial storefronts and informal vendor markets, resulting in struc-
tural inventory loss and municipal business paralysis[cite: 80, 82].
• Transportation and Road Asset Degradation: Prolonged sub-base saturation
beneath asphalt pavements accelerates stripping, pothole formation, and
structural foundation collapse[cite: 80, 82]. Subgrade soils in low-lying zones
lose shear strength when fully saturated, leading to multi-crore recurring
maintenance costs for municipal public works[cite: 80, 82].
• Public Health Hazards: Floodwaters mixed with choked drainage silt create
widespread standing pools, dramatically accelerating vector breeding cycles
during monsoon months[cite: 80, 82].
From an administrative perspective, municipal corporations possess strictly fi-

2.2 Digital Twins in Civil and Municipal Engineering
The paradigm of the Digital Twin (DT), originally conceived in aerospace and
advanced manufacturing by Grieves and Vickers, has rapidly expanded into civil
infrastructure and smart city operations[cite: 102]. A digital twin constitutes a
dynamic virtual counterpart of a physical asset or municipal system that maintains
continuous bi-directional synchronization through data ingestion, computational
analytics, and actionable operational feedback[cite: 102].
Fuller et al. categorize digital twins across three distinct evolutionary tiers[cite:
102]:
1. Digital Models: Static digital representations with manual data flow in both
directions (e.g., standard CAD/BIM repositories and static GIS maps)[cite:
102].
2. Digital Shadows: Systems wherein data flows automatically from the physi-
cal asset to the digital model via sensing devices or automated field surveys,
but operational interventions remain manual[cite: 102].

3. Digital Twins: Closed-loop cyber-physical systems wherein real-time sensory
or survey data updates the computational twin, and the twin generates
predictive interventions that directly drive physical actions (e.g., automated
control or prioritized field work orders)[cite: 102].

In an operational urban digital twin, the physical domain and virtual analytics
engine interact via a closed feedback loop:

In the water sector, digital twins have been predominantly deployed in pres-

this paradigm by establishing a digital twin of the Vellore stormwater system that
couples geospatial network models, surveyed sediment states, and dynamic storm
simulations to guide physical municipal desilting operations[cite: 102].
2.3 Machine Learning and Surrogate Modeling in Flood Risk Assessment
Given the prohibitive computational runtime of numerical 1D/2D hydrody-
namic models, researchers have turned to Machine Learning (ML) surrogate mod-

the input-output behavior of complex hydrodynamic simulations or empirical fail-

Kabir et al. demonstrated that deep neural architectures and ensemble decision
trees can predict urban inundation extents orders of magnitude faster than full 2D
shallow water solvers while preserving adequate accuracy[cite: 103]. Bermúdez et
al. utilized support vector machines and random forests trained on pre-calculated
hydraulic simulations to forecast localized water depths across river reaches in real
time[cite: 103].

6.2 Proposed Cascade-Aware Dispatch Strategy
To overcome the limitations of localized heuristics and exact NP-hard search,
CivicTwin introduces a multi-criteria lexicographical ranking framework termed
Cascade-Aware Prioritization. The algorithm evaluates all candidate con-
duits v∈ Vcand that are in the OPEN operational state, georeferenced within
municipal boundaries, and structurally eligible for excavation.
For every candidate conduit v, the strategy constructs a multi-variable lex-
icographical sort key:
Keycascade(v) = (−T (v, i),−Csaved(v),−U (v, i), v ) (6.5)
where the components are prioritized hierarchically:
1. Primary Priority Criterion — Categorical Threat Tier (−T (v, i)): Con-
duits are grouped first by hydraulic failure severity. All Critical seg-
ments ( T (v, i) = 2 , utilization U > 1.25, active surface overflow) are
scheduled strictly before High threat segments ( T (v, i) = 1 , 0.80 <
U≤ 1.25), which in turn precede Low threat segments ( T (v, i) = 0 ).

Within a shared threat tier, candidate conduits are ranked by their
upstream ancestor set cardinality |anc(v)|. A Critical conduit whose
desilting restores hydraulic relief to 1,300 upstream tributary conduits
is prioritized ahead of a Critical conduit that relieves only 20 upstream
conduits.
3. Tertiary Priority Criterion — Local Capacity Utilisation ( −U (v, i)):
For conduits tied in both threat tier and cascade reachability, priority
is assigned to the conduit carrying the highest local surcharge ratio
U (v, i).
4. Deterministic Tie-Breaker ( v): Stable tie-breaking is enforced using
unique internal segment indices to ensure repeatable, deterministic
queue generation.

8.1 Summary of Research Contributions
This dissertation has presented the design, implementation, and em-
pirical validation of CivicTwin, an AI-enabled cyber-physical digital
twin engineered to optimize predictive stormwater drainage resilience
for the Vellore City Municipal Corporation (CMC)[cite: 74, 119]. By
synthesizing geospatial information systems, hydraulic principles, com-
plex network graph theory, and machine learning, CivicTwin addresses
the systemic ineﬀiciencies of traditional reactive municipal desilting
operations[cite: 74, 83, 89, 119].
The key contributions of this research are[cite: 119]:
1. Urban Scale Drainage DAG Modeling: Successfully extracted and
structured 13,998 multi-modal stormwater conduit segments from
OpenStreetMap and elevation rasters into a topological Directed
Acyclic Graph (DAG) comprising 22,737 directed downhill edges
across 60 administrative zones[cite: 74, 83, 97, 119].
2. Bitset Reachability Engine: Developed a bitset-accelerated tran-
sitive closure algorithm over topological order that evaluates up-
stream ancestor reachability ( Csaved) in under 20 milliseconds, pro-
viding real-time visibility into backwater surcharge propagation[cite:
74, 99, 113, 119].
3. Machine Learning Blockage Surrogate: Formulated and evaluated
an ensemble Random Forest classifier achieving 89.4% cross-validated
accuracy in predicting structural blockage vulnerability from mor-
phometric, spatial, and topographic features[cite: 74, 104, 119].
4. Cascade-Aware Prioritization Algorithm: Formulated a multi-criteria
lexicographical ranking strategy that prioritizes conduits by threat
tier, upstream reachability, and local capacity utilization[cite: 74,
106, 119]. Simulation experiments across 80, 120, and 160 mm/hr
storm regimes demonstrated that the proposed method resolves
between 3.1x and 4.4x more over-capacity and backwater-affected
conduits than conventional severity-only municipal desilting under
identical maintenance budgets[cite: 74, 110, 119].

8.3 Limitations of the Current Study
Notwithstanding the promising empirical results, several limitations
must be acknowledged[cite: 120]:
∗ Hydrological Steady-State Assumption: Runoff is computed using
the rational method, which assumes a steady-state peak runoff rate
corresponding to a storm duration equal to the basin concentration
time[cite: 87, 96, 120]. While ideal for rapid operational ranking,
it does not simulate unsteady dynamic hydrograph propagation or
overland 2D surface inundation depths[cite: 87, 120].

across 14,000 conduits remains challenging[cite: 95, 120].
